value.text: 2000 vs 2026 Market Overlay S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 · daily closes · data through Nov 16, 2026 (intraday) The S&P 500 is tracking the 2000 top. The tech mania it rode on is not. Lined up on their peaks, the S&P 500's path into October 2026 and the six weeks after it look a lot like early 2000. The overlay holds for the S&P's shape. It breaks down on size: the 1990s rally was two to six times larger, much steeper into the top and far more volatile. Index S&P 500 Nasdaq-100 Line up on Peaks Catalysts Best fit Where the analogy holds and where it breaks Holds · S&P timing The recent S&P path is a near-copy of early 2000 I compared the last four years of S&P prices with every window in 1997–2002. The closest match ends on May 4, 2000, six weeks after the March 24 top (correlation 0.985). Counting 29 sessions from each peak, the S&P was down 6.2% in 2000. It is down 5.2% today. Breaks · size of the run The 1990s run was far bigger From its 1994 low the S&P rose 243% into the 2000 top. From the October 2022 low it rose 119%. For the Nasdaq-100 the gap is 1,237% against 192%. At its 2000 peak the Nasdaq-100 sat 56% above its 200-day average. In October 2026 it was 13% above. Breaks · tech timing On shape, tech looks like 1998 Run the same shape match on the Nasdaq-100 over three years and the best fit is late October 1998, not 2000. Tech has had nothing like the 1999 blow-off: that year the index doubled in twelve months, with volatility above 45%. Holds · valuation & concentration Prices are close to 2000 extremes The Shiller CAPE is about 39–40, against a record 44 in December 1999. The ten largest stocks make up about 38–40% of the S&P, against about 27% at the 2000 peak. The difference is that today's leaders earn a large share of index profits. Many 1999 leaders had little or no earnings. Then and now, side by side Measure S&P 2000 S&P 2026 Nasdaq-100 2000 Nasdaq-100 2026 Into the peak (Mar 24/27, 2000 · Oct 6, 2026) Gain from cycle low Lows: Dec 1994 / Jun 1994 · Oct 2022 / Dec 2022 +243% +119% +1,237% +192% Gain since catalyst Netscape IPO Aug 9, 1995 · ChatGPT Nov 30, 2022 +173% +92% +718% +160% Years from catalyst to peak 4.6 3.8 4.6 3.8 12-month return into peak +19.1% +16.4% +126.9% +26.0% 3-year annualized return into peak +24.6% +22.2% +77.8% +28.5% Distance above 200-day average +11.3% +8.1% +56.0% +13.4% 3-month realized volatility 24.1% 11.1% 47.1% 18.6% 29 sessions after the peak Change from peak May 4, 2000 · Nov 16, 2026 −6.2% −5.2% −25.1% −12.8% Market-wide (S&P 500) Shiller CAPE 44.2 (Dec 1999) · ~39–40 (Nov 2026) Top-10 share of index ~27% · ~38–40% What 2000 did next If the analogy holds, the S&P chart gives a sequence to watch for. A long, choppy top. Sixty sessions after the peak the S&P was only 3.4% lower. In September 2000 it came back to within 0.5% of the high. The real decline came later. One year after the peak the S&P was down 24.5%. The low came in October 2002, 49% below the top, 2½ years later. Tech fell first and hardest. The Nasdaq-100 lost 25% in the first six weeks and 83% by October 2002. Reasons to discount it Any two rising markets can be made to overlap if you pick the anchor dates. The peak-aligned view assumes October 6 was the top, which nobody knows yet. Today's S&P is 5.2% off its high. A drop that size is common: the index fell 18.9% from February to April 2025 and recovered. Five-year returns are also much lower now: 9.5% a year for the S&P versus 25% into 2000. The 2022 bear market partly reset the cycle, so this run is younger and smaller. The point of view that holds up is narrower: valuations and concentration are at levels where the 2000 outcome is possible, and the S&P's recent path has not ruled it out.
